# Evaluating Cell Membrane Localization and Intracellular Transport of Proteins by Biotinylation. Protein translocation to the cell membrane and transport through intracellular compartments are dynamic processes frequently altered in cancer cells. Abnormal protein localization can affect key cell functions, including transduction of extracellular signals and organization of the cytoskeleton, significantly affecting oncogenicity and therapeutic responses. In this chapter, we describe a surface protein biotinylation method that allows the study of membrane localization and endosomal transport of membrane-associated proteins. Further, the combination of this technique with other strategies, such as treatments with transport inhibitors, allows investigation of specific steps of protein trafficking through the cell. ### Cell Surface Protein Biotinylation for SDS-PAGE Analysis. ### Improved sensitivity in cell surface protein detection by combining chemical labeling with mechanical lysis in a colorectal cancer cell model. ### The Principles of Protein Targeting and Transport Across Cell Membranes. results.title: A Comprehensive Model for Separating Systematic Bias and Noise in Metabolomic Timecourse Data—A Nonlinear B‐Spline Mixed‐Effects Approach - Isaac - 2025 - Biotechnology and Bioengineering - Wiley Online Library
results.content: # A Comprehensive Model for Separating Systematic Bias and Noise in Metabolomic Timecourse Data—A Nonlinear B-Spline Mixed-Effects Approach. However, since systematic bias, by its definition, influences all metabolites within a sample in a similar fashion, it can be identified and corrected through the simultaneous fit of all detected metabolites in a single timecourse model. The proposed model was successfully applied to real cell culture data and validated using simulated timecourse data perturbed with varying degrees of random noise and systematic bias. Systematic bias is estimated as a nonlinear random effect that is combined with B-spline regression, which models the smoothly varying metabolite concentrations over time for each of the observed metabolites. where represents a scaling term that accounts for systematic bias across all metabolites in time point , represents a bias-free B-spline curve for each metabolite, and represents the remaining random error. Next, the analysis was expanded to include systematic errors at multiple points to assess the model's performance in handling both systematic bias and noise affecting all time points. For this, 100 simulations were generated, with all time points perturbed by noise and systematic bias derived from a random normal distribution with a standard deviation of 3%, 5%, or 10%. Moreover, the correction of systematic bias was observed to have a profound effect on the first derivative estimates across time points (Figure 2B), which is essential for accurate metabolic flux analysis. The accuracy and consistency of the proposed model in correcting systematic bias were first evaluated by fitting simulated timecourse datasets perturbed with a single biased point. Following single time point error correction, the proposed model was applied to a more realistic scenario where time points can be affected by a combination of random and systematic errors. This study presents a robust nonlinear mixed-effects model for correcting systematic error in timecourse metabolomic data. The model integrates an estimate of systematic bias directly into the timecourse fit, leveraging the structure of time-series data to distinguish between random noise and systematic error. Application to both real cell culture datasets and simulated datasets with known errors has demonstrated the model's ability to accurately correct a systematic bias of 3%-10% to within 0.5% on average for typical data.

results.title: Dopamine transporter cell surface localization facilitated by a direct interaction with the dopamine D2 receptor: Full Paper PDF & Summary | Bohrium
results.content: Dopamine transporter cell surface localization facilitated by a direct interaction with the dopamine D2 receptor. # Dopamine transporter cell surface localization facilitated by a direct interaction with the dopamine D2 receptor. **Research Direction:** dopamine transporter ｜ D2 receptor ｜ protein - protein interaction. The dopamine transporter (DAT) and D2 receptor are key components in dopaminergic neurotransmission. This study aims to explore the direct protein - protein interaction between DAT and D2 receptor and its functional consequences. D2 receptors and DAT form a protein complex. The E297 - Q344 region of the D2 receptor and the DAT NT1 [M1 - P26] region are responsible for mediating the interaction between the two proteins. Direct protein - protein interaction between D2 receptor and DAT. These results confirm the existence of a direct protein - protein interaction between the D2 receptor and DAT and the role of DAT M1 - V15 in this interaction. D2S receptors enhance DAT - mediated DA uptake through the D2 - DAT direct protein - protein interaction. Overexpression of mini - genes encoding DAT sequences responsible for the D2 receptor interaction blocked the D2S - receptor - mediated enhancement of DAT - mediated DA uptake. Experiments in rats treated with D2 receptor agonists or antagonists showed that the D2 - DAT physical interaction is agonist - independent. D2 receptors recruit DAT to plasma membrane through the D2 - DAT direct protein - protein interaction. The enhancement of DA uptake by D2S co - expression, without an increase in DAT protein levels, suggests recruitment of intracellular DAT to the plasma membrane. In midbrain neurons, application of relevant peptides affected DAT membrane expression, indicating that the D2 receptor enhances DAT membrane expression through the D2 - DAT interaction. Biotinylation experiments in HEK - 293 cells suggested that the D2 - DAT interaction facilitates DAT insertion into the plasma membrane rather than decreasing endocytosis. Here, we report that the DAT is also regulated by the dopamine D2 receptor through a direct protein-protein interaction involving the DAT amino-terminus and the third intracellular loop of the D2 receptor. Moreover, mice injected with peptides that disrupt D2-DAT interaction exhibit decreased synaptosomal dopamine uptake and significantly increased locomotor activity, reminiscent of DAT knockout mice.

results.title: Dopamine transporter cell surface localization facilitated by a direct interaction with the dopamine D2 receptor
results.content: To determine the functional relevance for the D2–DAT interaction, we examined how D2 receptors modulate DAT‐mediated DA uptake in HEK‐293 cells coexpressing D2S receptors and DAT. To investigate whether the observed D2 receptor‐mediated enhancement of DA uptake is the consequence of D2–DAT protein complex formation, in HEK‐293 cells coexpressing D2S and DAT, we overexpressed mini‐genes encoding DAT sequences that are responsible for the interaction with D2 receptors. Furthermore, overexpression of the DAT NT1‐1 mini‐gene, which encodes a peptide that has been shown to disrupt the D2–DAT interaction (Figure 1H), significantly blocked the D2S receptor‐mediated enhancement in DAT uptake (Figure 2E), providing evidence that sequences M 1‐V 15 of the DAT mediates the direct protein–protein interaction of D2–DAT and facilitates the D2S‐dependent enhancement of DAT‐mediated DA uptake. These data suggest that the D2 receptor enhances DAT membrane expression through the D2–DAT direct protein–protein interaction and the enhanced DAT‐mediated DA uptake may be a result of increased DAT plasma membrane expression. (**D**) Biotinylation of HEK‐293 cell surface proteins after treatment with 10 μM TAT peptides for 30 min at 37°C reveals an increase in DAT at the cell surface upon coexpression of the D2S receptor. Although we have almost exclusively used the D2S isoform in experiments involving transfected cells or GST fusion proteins, as the DAT coupling site located on the D2 receptor occurs in an area common for both D2S and D2L, we would not have been surprised if the D2L receptor was also capable of enhancing DAT uptake via a direct protein–protein interaction with DAT. Although D2 receptor knockout mice do not exhibit elevated dopamine levels (Dickinson _et al_, 1999), which at the surface would appear to contradict our model, this may be accounted for by the diversity of proteins capable of regulating the DAT (e.g. PICK1, Hic‐5 and α‐synuclein).
